overview.t: Ryan Fazio is a state senator and the nominee of the Republican and Independent parties for Governor.
His campaign website says that in the State Senate he has

overview.q: fought relentlessly to make Connecticut more affordable

overview.t: , and lists among his distinctions

overview.q: A lifetime perfect score from the CT Business and Industry Association

paras.t: His issues page says his plan would

paras.q: reduce state income-tax rates, providing more than $2.5 billion in annual tax relief when fully implemented

paras.t: It also says his plan would

paras.q: lower income taxes for every Connecticut family by $1,500 and implement property tax caps

paras.t: His tax plan page is headlined

paras.q: Fazio Announces Largest Middle-Class Tax Cut in Connecticut History

plan.t: Cut income tax rates by about 2 percentage points for most families, worth roughly $2.5 billion a year by the fourth year of his term (for example, 4.5% to 2.5% and 5.5% to 3.5%).

plan.q: wasteful and politically oriented spending by about $1 billion per year by 2031

plan.t: , including ending political earmarks and over-budgeting for agencies.

plan.q: Cap property tax increases at no greater than 2% or the rate of inflation
Require a 60% vote of the legislature for any legislation that creates new mandates or imposes additional costs on municipalities
Full expensing of capital expenditures to incentivize building factories, offices, buying machinery and plants

plan.t: CT Mirror reported that the plan relies partly on spending and revenue estimates from last November, and that the legislature’s nonpartisan analysts now project operating deficits.

paras.t: On housing, the site describes a plan that

paras.q: reduces the cost of housing, allows Connecticut to grow its housing supply, and protects local control of zoning and decision-making

plan.q: Streamline permitting processes to make them more rules-based, speedy, and predictable
Incentivize small-scale housing development and other housing with more community support, including Accessory Dwelling Units, residential in mixed-use areas, and more
Eliminate or roll back 8-30(g) and H.B. 8002 in a way that gives towns and cities more flexibility

paras.t: On energy costs, the site says he has a plan to

paras.q: cut electricity bills by 20%
ending hidden taxes, expanding reliable supply, and removing the mandates driving up costs

paras.t: It says he would end a state tax break for large data centers.

plan.t: Eliminate the Public Benefits Charge: end or sunset most of the 50-plus programs funded through it and move a small portion of the rest into the state budget.
End the Renewable Portfolio Standard and Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative charges in the supply portion of bills, or let nuclear and hydropower count toward the standard.

plan.q: Expand natural gas pipeline capacity from Pennsylvania
Have Connecticut officially intervene through the federal regulatory process at FERC or sue the State of New York if it continues to block pipeline expansion proposals
Limit any long-term contract for electricity to no more than a nominal difference from the wholesale market price of electricity
Eliminate special tax subsidies for data centers, EV chargers, and heat pump installations

paras.q: our reading achievement has fallen and our math achievement is barely above average
High standards for literacy education: Every Connecticut student should be able to read by 3rd grade
No smartphones in classrooms

plan.q: Materials must be oriented around proven Science of Reading
High-dosage tutoring for students who fall behind as a systematic intervention
No more social promotion: High schools cannot graduate students without teaching them how to read
Adequate, transparent, student-centered funding

paras.q: reforms the 2020 anti-police legislation, closes parole loopholes for violent offenders, and reinstates proactive policing

plan.q: reforms the 2020 anti-police legislation, closes parole loopholes for violent offenders, and reinstates proactive policing

paras.q: streamline veteran services, reduce costs, cut fees, recognize out-of-state licenses

plan.q: streamline veteran services, reduce costs, cut fees, recognize out-of-state licenses

said.context: CT Mirror profile of his 2024 state Senate race in Greenwich. His Democratic opponent had cited Fazio’s votes on guns and abortion; Fazio responded that Democrats were using them as wedge issues.

seg.q: Easing gun laws in Connecticut or restricting abortion in Connecticut is never -- is not -- going to happen. And Republicans in the legislature are not in favor of it, and Democrats in the legislature are not in favor of it

said.context: Same debate, asked about the Reproductive Freedom Defense Act (HB 5414), which he voted against.

seg.q: Like many complex regulatory issues, I could be wrong in the long run, and I am open to that possibility, but the evidence at that point made me concerned it would undermine health and safety

plan.t: The Greenwich Free Press reported he said he supports keeping abortion legal in Connecticut and would do more to expand access to oral contraceptives; he said

plan.q: I co-authored and passed a new law that will expand access to oral contraceptives in Connecticut

said.context: Same CT Mirror profile; the article says Fazio voted in 2023 against a bill updating Connecticut’s gun law and that he said he objected to one section of it.

seg.q: Easing gun laws in Connecticut or restricting abortion in Connecticut is never -- is not -- going to happen.

said.context: League of Women Voters Greenwich debate with Democratic challenger Nick Simmons, in answer to a question about whether any gun safety regulations have gone too far. Simmons had criticized Fazio’s vote against a 2023 gun bill.

seg.q: Connecticut has probably the second or third strongest guns safety laws in the country. I not only support those laws

plan.q: I spoke on the Senate floor that night, simply introducing three amendments that would strengthen that gun law. It would provide a state support system for School Resources Officers
reintroduce policies like consent searches that have taken hundreds of illegal guns off the street in Connecticut

plan.t: . The Greenwich Free Press also reported he said he supports enforcing the existing assault weapons ban.

said.context: Reacting to Gov. Lamont’s first general-election ad, which criticized Fazio’s opposition to a 2026 bill limiting ICE arrests in schools and places of worship.

seg.q: I think that the governor was wrong and radical in tying the hands of state and federal law enforcement in communicating with federal authorities in the case of people who are here illegally, who have been convicted of Class C, D and E felonies like manslaughter and sexual abuse

plan.t: He introduced Senate Bill 684, “An Act Repealing the Trust Act,” in the 2025 session; it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.

plan.q: My proposal is to repeal parts of the more radical version in 2019
detain and leverage federal authorities to protect our community from serious criminals in our country illegally
It’s not about knocking on every door, schools, or anything like that.

said.context: CT Mirror article on electricity and energy prices, discussing how the war in Iran has affected oil and gas costs.

seg.q: The governor of Connecticut doesn’t have any constitutional responsibilities or input on issues of war and peace
I always am rooting for a just and lasting peace

said.context: CT Mirror article on whether Connecticut should use state funds to replace expired federal ACA subsidies; Fazio opposes doing so.

seg.t: On using state money to offset the expired federal subsidies, he said it

seg.q: is literally just taking from taxpayers and not solving problems

plan.t: CT Mirror reported that his relief plan would end state-sponsored healthcare for undocumented adults and children, impose a “managed care” system to cap Medicaid assistance, and cut Medicaid spending by about $336 million a year by 2031.

plan.q: I have a proposal with 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans that would reform certificate of need laws
reduced healthcare costs by four to 10% and improved access

said.context: Joint statement from Fazio and three Greenwich state representatives, issued under the headline “Speak Out Against Homophobic, Transphobic Signs.”

seg.q: We’re shocked and saddened by this despicable act.

overview.t: Luke Bronin is the Democratic nominee in the 1st Congressional District, an open seat because incumbent Rep. John Larson lost his primary.
His campaign website says

overview.q: From 2016 to 2024, Luke served as the mayor of Hartford

overview.t: , and that he

overview.q: served as a Navy intelligence officer and deployed to Afghanistan

paras.q: Reproductive freedom is a basic human right. Congress must pass federal protections for abortion access nationwide.

plan.q: Congress must pass federal protections for abortion access nationwide.

plan.t: He says that as mayor he led an ordinance on crisis pregnancy centers that

plan.q: became a model for legislation in the state of Connecticut

paras.q: Every person deserves to live freely, safely, and with dignity, no matter who they love or how they identify.

plan.q: In Congress, I’ll fight to pass the Equality Act

plan.t: , enshrine protections for marriage equality, and support the Global Respect Act.

ensuring the wealthiest Americans and biggest corporations actually pay their fair share

plan.t: Close loopholes such as carried interest,

adding two new top income tax brackets
Make the capital gains tax more progressive
restoring the corporate tax rate back to the pre-Trump rate of 35% or at minimum to 28%

plan.q: We need a strong public option so that any American who wants to participate in Medicare can do so.
In the near term, we must pass the Break Up Big Medicine Act

plan.t: , a bipartisan bill to break up healthcare monopolies.

paras.q: outlined a plan to stop ICE’s lawlessness in the short term while working to abolish ICE from the ground up in the longer term

plan.t: , including a ban on masks, warrant requirements and visible identification for officers.

plan.q: Abolish ICE, which has only existed since 2003.
secure borders, fair and timely asylum processing, citizenship for DACA recipients, legal pathways that encourage more legal immigration

paras.q: High costs are crushing almost everyone but the wealthiest Americans
focus relentlessly to make life easier and more affordable

plan.q: We need to build more housing, produce cheaper renewable energy, and make sure markets actually work to give consumers real choices.

paras.q: Climate change isn’t some distant future threat. It’s now.

plan.q: We need a massive commitment to more affordable, clean energy. Solar, wind, hydro, fuel cells, nuclear, and building better batteries.
streamlining red tape that makes it too hard and costly to build

paras.q: universal background checks, an assault weapons ban, safe storage laws, red-flag laws

I’ll support vital community violence prevention work like violence interrupters and hospital-based violence intervention programs.
reverse the Trump administration’s damaging cuts to ATF

paras.q: expand support to quality classroom education across the country, from early childhood education all the way through to affordable pathways to college or skilled trades

smaller class sizes, stronger teacher training and recruitment, better teacher pay

overview.t: Joe Courtney, the incumbent, is the Democratic nominee in the 2nd Congressional District.
His official biography says he

overview.q: was elected in 2006 to represent the Second Congressional District of Connecticut

overview.t: and is

overview.q: Ranking Member of the House Armed Services Subcommittee on Seapower and Projection Forces

paras.q: worked to strengthen our nation's defense by leading the call for increased submarine production

plan.q: leading the call for increased submarine production
we now need to double down on the Manufacturing Pipeline Initiative’s success for decades to come

paras.t: In an October 9, 2026 op-ed he wrote

paras.q: I am a co-sponsor of the Lowering Drug Costs for American Families Act (H.R. 6166)
Congress should pass the Lowering Drug Costs for American Families Act into law

plan.q: Congress should pass the Lowering Drug Costs for American Families Act into law

plan.t: , a bill that would let Medicare negotiate drug prices for people on employer-based and ACA marketplace plans, not only those 65 and older.

paras.q: introduced and won passage of a law that designated the Eightmile River in Connecticut as a part of the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System
distinguished himself as a tireless advocate for both our nation's veterans and our men and women in uniform

said.context: Press statement issued the day the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.

seg.q: The decision released by the Supreme Court today overturning 50 years of settled law protecting the reproductive health decisions of women and families in the U.S. is a stunning step backwards for the privacy rights of all Americans

said.context: Press release after the House passed the Respect for Marriage Act, which he voted for.

seg.q: As consenting adults, Americans have the right to love who they choose, and to marry who they love

said.context: Press release after the House passed the Assault Weapons Ban Act of 2022 (217-213), which he voted for and co-sponsored.

seg.q: H.R. 1808 would restore the ban on military-style assault weapons that was formerly in place throughout our country during one of the most prosperous and low-crime points in American history.

plan.t: He co-sponsored and voted for the Assault Weapons Ban Act of 2022, which would prohibit the sale, manufacture, transfer or possession of semiautomatic assault weapons and high-capacity magazines.

said.context: Press statement on House passage of a Department of Homeland Security funding bill that excluded ICE and CBP funding.

seg.q: For 76 days, critical DHS agencies that have nothing to do with the out of control lawless actions of ICE have taken the brunt of this shutdown.

plan.q: I cosponsored a bill to fully fund all DHS agencies except for ICE and CBP

said.context: Press release marking ten years of the Manufacturing Pipeline Initiative in eastern Connecticut.

seg.q: we now need to double down on the Manufacturing Pipeline Initiative’s success for decades to come

plan.q: we now need to double down on the Manufacturing Pipeline Initiative’s success for decades to come

said.context: Remarks to Education Secretary Linda McMahon, shared in a press release about a federal rule on nursing student-loan caps.

seg.q: Your own data in terms of analyzing this rulemaking process actually showed that for nurse anesthetists, at least 28% of them who are in education right now have costs that exceed the [student loan] caps.

said.context: Press statement after he voted “no” on H.R. 1, the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”

seg.q: the Republican majority in Congress chose to jam through a partisan budget bill which gives a massive tax break to millionaires and billionaires and partially offsets it with the largest health care cut in U.S. history

plan.q: Like any law, it can be overturned, and over time, the will of the majority will ensure that it is.

overview.t: John Kissel is the incumbent on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 7, running as: Republican; Independent Party of Connecticut.

paras.q: John knows every state policy should help make Connecticut more affordable to live, work and raise a family.

plan.q: John is leading the fight for greater state support for special education teachers and programs, as well as early childhood education.

paras.q: John will continue to fight for more state dollars for local education.

overview.t: Rosa Aurelia Pepper-Macias is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 11, running as: Workers' Voice Party.

plan.q: Stop all ICE raids, detentions and deportations

paras.q: Abolish ICE!
STOP the war and use the Pentagon’s trillion-dollar budget for jobs, education, housing, food, and healthcare as rights

plan.q: No taxes on anyone earning $50,000 or less per year
Tax all income above $250,000 at 95% (when federal income tax is included)

paras.q: Socialize and expand healthcare: For a unified public healthcare plan

plan.q: Re-establish all gender affirming care at all CT hospitals and make it free, as a human right

paras.q: Equal rights for all regardless of their gender identity. Free access to gender-affirming care for all.
Contraception, abortion and other reproductive services free and on demand
Make all public colleges and universities tuition free
Workers' control over production to combat climate change and provide for human need, not for war, genocide and big tech authoritarianism
End unemployment with a shortened workweek compensated at full-time pay.

Patch: Candidate Profile: John-Paul Dorais, 17th State Senate District (Oct. 16, 2026)

overview.t: John-Paul Dorais is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 17, running as: Republican; Independent Party of Connecticut.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “What do you believe is the No. 1 issue facing Connecticut, and how do you plan to address it?”

seg.q: I would support meaningful tax relief, efforts to control property-tax growth, reducing unnecessary regulations and fees, and policies that make Connecticut more competitive for businesses and working families.

plan.q: Cap annual municipal property-tax levy increases at the greater of 2% or inflation, while allowing voters to approve exceptions for major projects.
Reduce Connecticut's Paid Family Leave payroll tax by 20%.

plan.t: His site cites a Senate Republican package that included

plan.q: a $1 billion working- and middle-class income tax cut

paras.q: Connecticut families work hard for their money. They should not have to watch more of every paycheck disappear into taxes while state government continues to grow.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Energy costs have been soaring in Connecticut. What are your plans to help address this issue?”

seg.q: I support reviewing programs currently funded through electric bills and determining which legitimate state programs should instead go through the normal state budget process

plan.q: A moratorium on data centers should be considered as an option.
I also support reasonable limits on costly power-purchase agreements and requiring legislative approval before PURA creates new programs that increase costs for ratepayers.

paras.q: Connecticut families shouldn't dread opening their electric bills.
proposed public-safety exceptions to legislation restricting cooperation with federal authorities

plan.q: recruiting and retaining qualified officers

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Affordability has been a major topic across the country and here in Connecticut. How do you plan to address this issue?”

seg.q: We also need to expand opportunities for skilled trades and apprenticeships so young people have pathways to good-paying careers without assuming a four-year college degree is the only option.

paras.q: Protect Local Control of Housing Policy

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “What do you believe is the No. 1 issue facing Connecticut, and how do you plan to address it?”

seg.q: The number one issue facing Connecticut families is affordability.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Affordability has been a major topic across the country and here in Connecticut. How do you plan to address this issue?”

seg.q: we also need to do more in terms of tax cuts, such as completely eliminating the state income tax on Social Security

look at other taxes like the property tax on motor vehicles

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “What do you believe is the No. 1 issue facing Connecticut, and how do you plan to address it?”

overview.t: Jason Guidone is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 19, running as: Republican.

paras.q: I support responsible spending, transparency in government, and policies that keep taxes under control.
I support strong parental involvement, a rigorous curriculum, and keeping education decisions in local hands
Making Connecticut more affordable so families, retirees, and young people can afford to stay here.

overview.t: Lee Elci is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 20, running as: Republican; Independent Party of Connecticut.

plan.q: Enact permanent, broad-based middle-class tax cuts, funded by real spending cuts, not gimmicks.
Impose a strict spending cap tied to inflation and population growth.
Ban hidden fee and tax hikes buried in budget implementer bills.

paras.q: Connecticut families are being taxed and priced out of their own state — while Hartford sits on surpluses instead of delivering relief.

plan.q: Restore real legal protections for officers acting in good faith.

paras.q: The 2020 police accountability law turned our officers into suspects instead of protectors, and it's driving good men and women out of the profession.

plan.q: Get public-benefit charges off your electric bill, keep Millstone working, and modernize the grid.

overview.t: Carolann Reid is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 21, running as: Democratic.

paras.q: Affordability and economic security are central challenges for District 21 and Connecticut.

plan.q: I will advocate for a state child tax credit, meaningful property-tax relief, more affordable child care, and workforce development that connects residents to sustainable careers.
I will push for greater scrutiny of utility costs, transparent electricity-rate decisions, and more affordable energy supplies without sacrificing reliability.

overview.t: Alma Sarelli is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 26, running as: Republican; Independent Party of Connecticut.
In a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey answered in 2022, they wrote:

overview.q: Alma Sarelli is a working mom who moved to Connecticut 13 years ago.

overview.t: The Westport Journal reported that League of Women Voters debates in the district were canceled because Sarelli's campaign said she would not participate or she did not respond to invitations, and that she did not respond to the Journal's request for comment.

said.context: Statement after winning the Republican nomination, as reported by the Westport Journal.

seg.q: Decisions affecting our towns should be made by locally elected officials, not transferred by state politicians to bureaucrats in Hartford

plan.q: fight to protect local zoning authority, oppose unfunded mandates, and require infrastructure planning before major development moves forward

paras.t: Her issues page says her campaign is focused on

paras.q: making Connecticut more affordable, protecting local control, preserving educational excellence, and strengthening support for special education

plan.q: oppose unfunded mandates
protect taxpayers
support excellent schools, require clear cost controls, improve traffic and parking planning, protect neighborhoods, and keep residents involved before major decisions are made
push for more responsible state support for education and special education

paras.q: strong schools and taxpayer accountability must go together

Sam Nestor for State Senate: Vision
Westport Journal: Westport LWV debate is latest cancelled reportedly for Sarelli’s non-participation (Oct. 9, 2026)

overview.t: Sam Nestor is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 26, running as: Democratic.
The Westport Journal reported that League of Women Voters debates in the district were canceled after the Republican candidate did not take part; Nestor said she was

overview.q: disappointed

overview.t: that she would not get to debate.

paras.q: I am absolutely committed to protecting civil rights, free speech, equality, women's rights, bodily autonomy, LGBTQIA+ rights, healthcare, voting rights, religious freedoms, and freedom of the press
I am absolutely committed to protecting civil rights, free speech, equality, women's rights, bodily autonomy, LGBTQIA+ rights, healthcare, voting rights, religious freedoms, and freedom of the press

plan.q: I will work to hold insurers accountable, to ensure it’s not just urban centers that have access to quality care, and find solutions to ever rising costs

paras.q: Healthcare costs are one of the main drivers of municipal budgets, school budgets, the cost of running a business, and our own household budgets.

plan.q: fully funding special education
I will promote and support alternative pathways to work, though career training, community college, and trade schools

paras.q: outstanding public education is near and dear to my heart

plan.q: I will advocate for increased funding for programs that bridge the gap on energy bills for those who can’t make ends meet
we need to double down on renewable energy sources
I will propose policies that make it easier for homeowners, businesses, and towns to build renewable energy capacity

paras.q: The cost of energy is an enormous burden for households, businesses, and government.

plan.q: if we don’t make it profitable for builders to build, lots remain undeveloped
we can help lower administrative costs for builders without sacrificing environmental or regulatory compliance

paras.q: Solving the housing crisis in Connecticut is key to solving the affordability crisis

overview.t: Rob Blanchard is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 28, running as: Democratic; Independent Party of Connecticut.
In a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey answered in 2024, they wrote:

overview.q: Rob is running to turn the 28th State Senate District blue for the first time in 50 years, because residents of the district have been underserved and underrepresented.

overview.t: He describes himself, in the Patch questionnaire, as having served as

overview.q: Governor Lamont's communications director

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Why are you seeking this office?”

seg.q: towns should take the lead on where and how they grow

plan.q: reform 830-g, repurpose existing buildings, and protect our watershed and open space from overdevelopment
we must invest in a workforce that attracts and trains the next generation of teachers, health care and public safety professionals, mental health workers, and manufacturers

paras.q: focused on making Connecticut more affordable by tackling the rising costs of housing, healthcare, and childcare, while supporting strong schools and vibrant local communities

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). Same answer.

seg.q: I’ll support letting small employers join together to buy coverage at a lower price, with the key ACA protections intact.

said.context: Quoted in CT News Junkie’s report on his campaign announcement.

seg.q: Every kid deserves pre-K, families need an affordable public healthcare option they can actually count on, and we have to hold utility companies accountable.

plan.q: push down the cost of prescriptions, protect and strengthen paid family and medical leave, and invest in and expand our childcare endowment

paras.q: tackling the rising costs of housing, healthcare, and childcare

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Why are you seeking this office?”

seg.q: defend our fundamental rights, such as a woman’s right to reproductive freedom and access to paid family and medical leave, regardless of who is in the White House

plan.q: I will fund public safety, strengthen red flag gun laws that save lives, and pass gun safety laws.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “What do you believe is the No. 1 issue facing Connecticut, and how do you plan to address it?”

seg.q: I’ll back tax relief that puts money straight into family budgets, like the Earned Income Tax Credit, the Child Tax Credit, and the property tax credit.

plan.q: I’ll fight for more municipal aid and bonding so our towns can fund their schools without reaching deeper into homeowners’ pockets.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Energy costs have been soaring in Connecticut. What are your plans to help address this issue?”

seg.q: I’ll start by protecting what’s working: the fixed-price nuclear contracts that shield us from price spikes, and the new rule that stops utilities from billing customers for lobbying, PR, and political donations.

plan.q: Then I’ll go line by line through the public benefits charge.
Anything that doesn’t earn its place on your bill should go.
Every kid deserves pre-K

paras.t: His site says he is running to

paras.q: tax the ultra-rich
Taxing the ultra-rich their fair share isn’t about class warfare or punishing success.
Healthcare in Connecticut shouldn’t feel like a luxury. It should be a guarantee that every family can see a doctor, fill a prescription, and get the care they need without fear of financial ruin.
Every human being deserves the right to lead happy, healthy and dignified lives, regardless of economic or immigration statuses.

paras.t: A Planned Parenthood Votes–Connecticut endorsement posted on his site says

paras.q: Aaron Zimmer will defend our right to choose.
Lowering costs for Connecticut families is about more than just taxes and energy bills.

overview.t: Eric Berthel is the incumbent on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 32, running as: Republican.

paras.q: He is a fierce advocate for public school education on all levels - student outcomes, teacher recruitment, funding and curriculum.
He is also outspoken about parental choice in education, including support of families who chose to homeschool their children.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire from his 2024 re-election campaign (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Why are you seeking this office?”

seg.q: My work has been focused on lowering taxes, lowering the cost of living, attracting new businesses and keeping our communities safe.

plan.q: I will continue to fight to reduce the burden caused by each of these issues.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire from his 2024 re-election campaign (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “What are the major differences between you and the other candidates?”

seg.q: I am a fiscal conservative who believes in smaller government, local control, lower taxes and creating opportunity for people to succeed

overview.t: Matthew Knickerbocker is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 32, running as: Democratic.
In a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey answered in 2026, they wrote:

overview.q: I am a former First Selectman and Board of Education chair for the Town of Bethel.

plan.q: Matt will fight to secure our fair share of state funding so local taxpayers aren’t left filling the gap.
Matt will push for full reimbursement of excess special education costs

paras.q: Every child deserves a strong public education, no matter their ZIP code.

plan.q: Matt will work to end this practice and ensure municipalities aren’t stuck covering costs for decisions made in Hartford.

paras.q: The state shouldn’t pass requirements without paying for them.

plan.q: Matt will work to cut red tape

overview.t: Brandi Mandato is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 34, running as: Democratic; Working Families.
In a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey answered in 2024, they wrote:

overview.q: Born and raised in Greater New Haven, the grand-daughter of Italian American immigrants, I grew up in a working class family, the oldest of eight children, and have watched the people I love work hard to find stability and build beautiful lives in Connecticut.

paras.t: Her site says her work has focused on

paras.q: to expand access to quality jobs, education pathways, including apprenticeships, trade schools, and higher education, and economic opportunity

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “What do you believe is the No. 1 issue facing Connecticut, and how do you plan to address it?”

seg.q: I will fight to reform Connecticut’s tax code so that the wealthiest individuals and most profitable corporations pay their fair share, while providing meaningful tax relief to working families and small businesses.

plan.q: reforming Connecticut’s tax code to provide meaningful relief for working families and small businesses while asking the wealthiest individuals and most profitable corporations to contribute their fair share

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Energy costs have been soaring in Connecticut. What are your plans to help address this issue?”

seg.q: I support giving municipalities and regional entities more flexibility to own and operate electric utilities, expanding access to affordable locally generated power, and making it easier for communities to pursue alternatives to investor-owned utilities.

plan.q: I support giving municipalities and regional entities more flexibility to own and operate electric utilities, expanding access to affordable locally generated power, and making it easier for communities to pursue alternatives to investor-owned utilities.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Affordability has been a major topic across the country and here in Connecticut. How do you plan to address this issue?”

seg.q: It means fully funding public education, expanding access to affordable childcare and paid family leave, protecting affordable housing, tackling healthcare and medical debt, and addressing the high cost of energy.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Affordability has been a major topic across the country and here in Connecticut. How do you plan to address this issue?”

seg.q: fully funding public education

overview.t: Paul Cicarella, Jr. is the incumbent on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 34, running as: Republican; Independent Party of Connecticut.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Affordability has been a major topic across the country and here in Connecticut. How do you plan to address this issue?”

seg.q: My focus is simple: keep more money in people’s pockets, control state spending, and make Connecticut a place where families can afford to live, work, and retire.

plan.q: Eliminating the Highway Use Tax
Eliminating Sales Tax on Meals sold at Grocery Stores
Implementing a Gas Tax Holiday

plan.t: are among the measures he lists.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Energy costs have been soaring in Connecticut. What are your plans to help address this issue?”

seg.q: eliminate the Public Benefits Charge on electric bills, cap long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) to prevent ratepayers from being locked into contracts at prices substantially above market rates, and return all proceeds from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) directly to ratepayers through electricity-bill relief

plan.q: eliminate the Public Benefits Charge on electric bills, cap long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) to prevent ratepayers from being locked into contracts at prices substantially above market rates, and return all proceeds from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) directly to ratepayers through electricity-bill relief

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Why are you seeking this office?” He listed what he would focus on if re-elected.

seg.q: Protecting local control by ensuring decisions reflect the needs of our communities, not one-size-fits-all mandates from Hartford.

said.context: Patch candidate questionnaire (answers written by the candidate). In answer to “Why are you seeking this office?”

seg.q: Delivering funding for our schools and fighting for a fairer education funding system.

overview.t: Jill Oberlander is a candidate on the November 3, 2026 ballot for State Senate District 36, running as: Democratic.

said.context: Round Hill Association debate (Oct. 7, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press. Asked about data centers.

seg.q: I think New York has the right approach. I think we should pause consideration on any data center

plan.q: Strengthen utility accountability and transparency in the rate-setting process.
Audit ratepayer-funded programs and protect effective energy-assistance programs.

paras.q: ratepayers deserve greater transparency and accountability

said.context: League of Women Voters Greenwich debate (Oct. 14, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press.

seg.q: I would work hard to bring money back to our district and I would not support new taxes

plan.q: Oppose broad-based tax increases and maintain Connecticut’s fiscal guardrails.
Reduce state-to-local cost shifting that puts pressure on property taxes.

paras.q: fiscal discipline and strong public services can go hand in hand

said.context: Round Hill Association debate (Oct. 7, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press. Asked what she would change about the 8-30g affordable housing law.

seg.q: What I won’t do is give into pressure to support bills that aren’t good for our community. I will be an advocate for our district and our local zoning laws.

plan.q: Cut unnecessary red tape for businesses.
Expand apprenticeships and workforce training that lead to jobs.
In Hartford, I want to be the liaison between the municipalities and the State to ensure we’re getting the support we need and to push back and fight against overreach on the part of the state.

paras.q: we should make it easier and less expensive to start and grow a business here

plan.q: Strengthen state support for local schools and improve Educational Cost Sharing funding.
Increase support for special education so local taxpayers aren’t left carrying disproportionate costs.

paras.q: the state should be a reliable funding partner

plan.q: Expand insurance-pooling options for small businesses and nonprofits.
Work to reduce premiums for families who purchase their own coverage.

paras.q: The rising cost of healthcare is straining families, seniors, small businesses and self-employed residents.

said.context: League of Women Voters Greenwich debate (Oct. 14, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press. Asked about reproductive rights and abortion; she said her father was an OB/GYN.

seg.q: These days it goes beyond saying, ‘I support the right to choose,’

seg.t: and added it was also important to support doctors, healthcare providers and access to services including prescriptions and counseling.

said.context: League of Women Voters Greenwich debate (Oct. 14, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press. Asked whether she would have supported the 2026 convertible-pistol law.

seg.q: And I will vote that way for any gun violence prevention bill. Anything that will keep our children and residents safe from gun violence, I will be a strong supporter of.

seg.q: I’m pro-choice
I was brought up as a Catholic with 16 years of Catholic education. I have three strong daughters and a strong wife. There’s no way I can argue any other way.

said.context: League of Women Voters Greenwich debate (Oct. 14, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press. Asked whether he would have supported the 2026 law (Public Act 26-41) banning pistols that can easily be converted into automatic weapons.

said.context: Round Hill Association debate (Oct. 7, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press. Asked about the state’s unfunded pension liabilities.

seg.q: We have to take bold moves in order to fix that by stimulating business. How do we do that? By lowering taxes

plan.q: You have to cut the taxes.

plan.t: The Greenwich Free Press also reported he talked about removing the public benefit charge from electricity bills.

said.context: Round Hill Association debate (Oct. 7, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press.

seg.q: Jobs are leaving, we can’t have that. We have to stimulate the state by making it more attractive

plan.q: I think 8-30g has created an adversarial relationship between the municipalities and Hartford
We’d vote it out
If elected, I will continue working to ensure Connecticut lives within its means while strengthening the communities we call home.

said.context: Round Hill Association debate (Oct. 7, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press. Asked about rising health insurance premiums.

seg.q: Healthcare should be a right, but I can’t have health care be run by the government because the government doesn’t run things well.

said.context: Round Hill Association debate (Oct. 7, 2026) between Joe Kelly and Jill Oberlander, as reported by the Greenwich Free Press. Asked about federal funding cuts to healthcare and education.

seg.q: We do have to make sure we fund our schools.
whatever is going to happen with federal funding, we have to have to make up for it with the state, because we can’t put our schools at risk

plan.q: we have to have to make up for it with the state, because we can’t put our schools at risk
